sections.h2: What a transfer on death deed is
sections.html:
It is a deed that names who gets a house when the owner dies, signed and recorded while the owner is alive. Maryland's version took effect October 1, 2026, under House Bill 738, Chapter 751 of the 2026 laws.

The new subtitle sits in Real Property Article 14-1001 and following. The owner stays in control for life: the deed gives the named beneficiary no ownership until death. It works much like a beneficiary designation on a bank account or life insurance policy.

The Act applies to a deed made before, on or after October 1, 2026, if the owner dies on or after that date. Talk with an estate planning attorney about drafting and recording, and about how the deed fits with a will and the rest of the plan.

  • Owner: called the transferor in the statute.
  • Beneficiary: the person or people named to receive the property.
  • Joint owners: owners with survivorship rights, such as tenants by the entirety, are treated differently from tenants in common.

sections.h2: Who can sign one and what it must say
sections.html:
Any owner with the capacity needed to make a will can sign one. The deed must follow the execution rules in Estates and Trusts 4-101 and must state that the transfer to the beneficiary happens at the owner's death.

The statutory form in 14-1011 includes owner and beneficiary information, a legal description, the transfer-at-death statement, and preparer and notary sections. Witnesses and notaries can't be relatives of the owners or beneficiaries, or beneficiaries themselves.

A deed can name one beneficiary or several. If it names several without saying how they hold title, they take as joint tenants with rights of survivorship. A deed can also name alternate beneficiaries, including successive alternates, who take if a primary beneficiary doesn't survive the owner.

The deed must be recorded in the land records of the county where the house sits before the owner dies, or it has no effect. Signing it is not enough.

Recording follows Real Property 3-104 with several changes the Act makes for TOD deeds. The collector's endorsement, certain intake sheet and assessment office endorsements, and the attorney or party preparation certification don't apply. The clerk may still refuse a TOD deed that comes without an intake sheet. The assessment records don't change to the beneficiary's name until the owner's death.

When it takes effectAt the owner's death, if recorded before then

The exemptions rest on Tax-Property 12-108, 13-207 and 13-414.

sections.h2: What the owner can still do while alive
sections.html:
Almost everything. The deed doesn't change the owner's right to live in, sell or mortgage the house, and it doesn't give the beneficiary a legal or equitable interest.

Section 14-1007 spells out what a recorded TOD deed doesn't do during the owner's life.

  • It doesn't limit the owner's right to sell or encumber the property.
  • It doesn't affect a buyer's or lender's rights, even if they know about the deed.
  • It doesn't affect the rights of the owner's creditors, including future ones.
  • It doesn't affect eligibility for public assistance, including Medicaid, for the owner or the beneficiary.
  • It doesn't expose the house to claims by the beneficiary's creditors.

That is a real difference from adding a relative to the title as a joint owner, which can expose the house to that person's creditors, lawsuits or divorce and gives them present rights.

You change or revoke it by recording a new document before the owner dies. A TOD deed is always revocable, even if the deed itself says otherwise.

There are three ways to revoke all or part of a recorded deed, each recorded in the county land records.

  • A new TOD deed that expressly revokes the earlier one or conflicts with it.
  • An instrument of revocation that says so expressly.
  • A lifetime deed that expressly revokes the TOD deed.

A will can't revoke a recorded TOD deed, and neither can marking up the deed itself. With joint owners, a deed is revoked only if all living joint owners revoke. A TOD deed naming a spouse is revoked automatically by divorce or annulment, and it is also revoked if the owner later marries and has a child by birth, adoption or legitimation.

sections.h2: What happens when the owner dies
sections.html:
Title passes to the surviving beneficiary by operation of law, without probate for that house. The beneficiary takes subject to any existing mortgage, lien, security interest or encumbrance, and the transfer carries no warranty of title.

If a beneficiary doesn't survive the owner, that share lapses, and an alternate takes if one is named. A beneficiary who intentionally killed the owner is disqualified, and the Act keeps the rights of pretermitted children and the elective share of a spouse in play. Any beneficiary may disclaim, and for real property the disclaimer must be recorded in the county land records.

Section 14-1013 creates an optional Notification of Death form. The statute sets no deadline to record it, and the transfer happens at death whether or not it is recorded. Recording it still matters, because the clerk forwards it to the State Department of Assessments and Taxation so the property records can be updated. If a beneficiary who lives in the house uses the form's occupancy option, the beneficiary certifies under penalty of perjury to live there as a principal residence for at least 7 of the next 12 months.

sections.h2: Selling a house held under a TOD deed
sections.html:
The owner can sell the house any time while alive without the beneficiary's consent. After death, the beneficiary can sell once title has passed and the paperwork is in order.

A beneficiary who inherits through a TOD deed takes a house with whatever debt is attached. A buyer or title company may ask to see the recorded TOD deed and the notification of death, if one was recorded. Gather the recorded deed, a certified death certificate and any mortgage statement before you list, so the closing doesn't stall on paperwork.

Cash Home Buyers buys Maryland houses as-is, including inherited homes. If you are a beneficiary and the house needs repairs or has back taxes, call us before you spend money on repairs. If you are an owner thinking about a TOD deed and a sale, remember that the deed doesn't stop you from selling while you are alive.

Before relying on a TOD deed, check the tax effects, existing liens, multiple beneficiaries, possible family disputes and Medicaid or long-term care planning.

faqs.q: When did Maryland's transfer on death deed take effect?
faqs.a: October 1, 2026, under House Bill 738 (Chapter 751 of the 2026 laws). It covers deeds made before, on or after that date if the owner dies on or after it.

faqs.q: Does a TOD deed have to be recorded?
faqs.a: Yes. It is effective only if recorded in the land records of the county where the property is located before the owner's death.

faqs.q: Can I still sell my house if I record a TOD deed?
faqs.a: Yes. The deed doesn't limit your right to sell or mortgage the property, and it doesn't give the beneficiary any interest while you are alive.

faqs.q: Does a will override a TOD deed in Maryland?
faqs.a: No. A recorded TOD deed can't be revoked by a will. It can be revoked by a recorded new TOD deed, a recorded revocation, or a recorded lifetime deed.

faqs.q: Does a TOD deed avoid inheritance tax?
faqs.a: No. The recordation and transfer taxes are exempt for a residence, but beneficiaries may still owe inheritance tax.
